source: At 48–50 hpf, melanophores were detected in Cluster eight based on expression of mitfa, dct, tyrp1b, and pmela (Du et al., 2003; Lister et al., 1999; Ludwig et al., 2004; Quigley and Parichy, 2002; Figure 1F; Figure 2A), also reflected by the dot and tSNE plots (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis supported by citations.

claim: At 68–70 hpf, discrete pigment cell populations were resolved that included xanthophore, iridophore, and two distinct melanophore clusters.
source: At 68–70 hpf, we resolved discrete pigment cell populations that included xanthophore, iridophore, and two distinct melanophore clusters (Figure 2D–G, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The xanthophores mapped to Cluster 15 and were enriched with xdh, aox5, pax7b, mitfa, and gch2.
source: The xanthophores mapped to Cluster 15 and were enriched with xdh, aox5, pax7b, mitfa, and gch2 (Nord et al., 2016; Parichy et al., 2000; Saunders et al., 2019; Minchin and Hughes, 2008; Lister et al., 1999; Figure 2A,D,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis supported by citations.

claim: Cluster 16 was identified as iridophores, which presented the markers tfec, pnp4a, gpnmb, and atic.
source: Cluster 16 was identified as iridophores, which presented the well-characterized markers: tfec, pnp4a, gpnmb, and atic (Higdon et al., 2013; Lister et al., 2011; Petratou et al., 2018; Petratou et al., 2019; Figure 2A,D,G; Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis supported by citations.

claim: Two different melanophore clusters at 68–70 hpf (Clusters 4 and 18) were present in different proliferative states.
source: The use of cell cycle markers revealed that two different melanophore clusters at 68–70 hpf (Clusters 4 and 18) were present in different proliferative states (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the cell cycle analysis.

claim: Cluster 18 expressed S and G2/M markers, such as pcna and aurkb, suggesting this population to be proliferating melanophores.
source: While the majority of cells in Cluster four were in G1, Cluster 18 expressed S and G2/M markers, such as pcna and aurkb, suggesting this population to be proliferating melanophores (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,E,F; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cell cycle data.

claim: At 68–70 hpf, a pigment progenitor population was identified where iridophore and melanophore markers were co-expressed in Cluster 13.
source: At 68–70 hpf, we identified a pigment progenitor population, where iridophore and melanophore markers were co-expressed in Cluster 13 (Figure 2A,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Undifferentiated pigment progenitor cells expressed tfec in combination with mitfa.
source: These undifferentiated pigment progenitor cells expressed tfec in combination with mitfa and have been described recently at 24, 30, and 48 hpf (Petratou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis supported by a citation.

claim: Cluster 13 expressed tfap2e, gpx3, and trpm1b.
source: Additionally, Cluster 13 expressed tfap2e, gpx3, and trpm1b (Figure 1—source data 2) whose expression patterns have been previously reported in pigment progenitors (Saunders et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis supported by a citation.

claim: A population of pigmented muscle (Cluster 9) was found with a weak melanophore signature coupled with expression of the muscle markers ckmb, tpma, tnnc2, and tnnt3b.
source: Finally, a population of pigmented muscle (Cluster 9) was also found with a weak melanophore signature coupled with expression of the muscle markers ckmb, tpma, tnnc2, and tnnt3b (Figure 1—source data 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: At 48–50 hpf, sox10:GFP+ cells that expressed mitfa were identified as melanophores.
source: When examining mitfa and tfec at 48–50 hpf (Figure 2H), we detected sox10:GFP+ cells that expressed mitfa, identifying the melanophores (Figure 2H; white arrowhead), and cells that expressed both mitfa and tfec, defining the pigment progenitors (Figure 2H; red arrowhead).
evidence: This is a finding from the HCR validation.

claim: At 48–50 hpf, cells that expressed both mitfa and tfec were identified as pigment progenitors.
source: When examining mitfa and tfec at 48–50 hpf (Figure 2H), we detected sox10:GFP+ cells that expressed mitfa, identifying the melanophores (Figure 2H; white arrowhead), and cells that expressed both mitfa and tfec, defining the pigment progenitors (Figure 2H; red arrowhead).
evidence: This is a finding from the HCR validation.

claim: At 68–70 hpf, four distinct pigment populations were confirmed: GFP+ melanophores expressing mitfa only, iridophores only expressing tfec, pigment progenitors expressing both mitfa and tfec, and sox10:GFP+ xanthophores expressing both xdh and mitfa.
source: At 68–70 hpf, we confirmed the four distinct pigment populations we identified through Seurat (Figure 2B–G):GFP+ melanophores expressing mitfa only (Figure 2I; white arrowhead), iridophores only expressing tfec (Figure 2I; blue arrowhead), and pigment progenitors expressing both mitfa and tfec (Figure 2I; red arrowhead) were detected. When examining xdh and mitfa expression patterns, sox10:GFP+ xanthophores were found to be expressing both markers (Figure 2J; orange arrowhead).
evidence: This is a finding from the HCR validation.

claim: Mesenchyme cells expressed twist1a, prrx1a/b, twist1b, foxc1a/b, snai1a/b, cdh11, sparc, colec12, meox1, pdgfra.
source: In addition to twist1a, mesenchyme cells also expressed prrx1a/b, twist1b, foxc1a/b, snai1a/b, cdh11, sparc, colec12, meox1, pdgfra (Figure 3A,B), and other known mesenchymal markers such as mmp2 (Figure 1—source data 2; Janssens et al., 2013; Theodore et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis supported by citations.

claim: Broad expression of foxc1a and mmp2 was observed along the posterior pharyngeal arches and ventral regions of the embryo at 48 hpf via in situ hybridization.
source: In whole mount embryos at 48 hpf, we observed broad expression of foxc1a and mmp2 along the posterior pharyngeal arches and ventral regions of the embryo via in situ hybridization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D; arrowheads), confirming their expression territories within posterior-ventral mesenchymal tissues.
evidence: This is a finding from the in situ hybridization validation.

claim: Nine clusters with chondrogenic signatures were detected among sox10:GFP+ cells with a mesenchymal identity.
source: Further analysis revealed various transcriptionally-distinct populations were present among the sox10:GFP+ cells with a mesenchymal identity. Among these, we detected nine clusters with chondrogenic signatures—identified by expression of mesenchymal signature genes, as well as the chondrogenic markers barx1 and/or dlx2a (Sperber et al., 2008; Sperber and Dawid, 2008; Ding et al., 2013; Barske et al., 2016; Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis supported by citations.

claim: Within the nine chondrogenic clusters, gene expression indicated heterogeneous cell states, ranging from proliferative, progenitor/stem-like, and migratory to differentiating signatures.
source: Within the nine chondrogenic clusters, we discovered gene expression indicative of heterogeneous cell states, ranging from proliferative, progenitor/stem-like, and migratory to differentiating signatures (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Cluster 14 at 48 hpf and Clusters 1 and 7 at 68–70 hpf exhibited a general mesenchymal signature and also expressed fin bud marker genes (hand2, tbx5a, hoxd13a, prrx1a).
source: Cluster 14 at 48 hpf and Clusters 1 and 7 at 68–70 hpf exhibited a general mesenchymal signature, but also expressed fin bud marker genes (hand2, tbx5a, hoxd13a, prrx1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 5; Yelon et al., 2000; Lu et al., 2019; Nakamura et al., 2016; Feregrino et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis supported by citations.

claim: The co-expression of prrx1b, twist1a, and barx1 was confirmed within sox10:GFP+ domains along the posterior pharyngeal arches and fin bud mesenchyme at both time points using HCR analysis.
source: To confirm the spatial co-expression of prrx1b, twist1a, and barx1 within sox10:GFP+ tissues, we utilized HCR analysis (Figure 3F–K,M–R). Corroborating our analysis that mesenchyme-identity populations contained both general and chondrogenic signatures, we found the co-expression of prrx1b, twist1a, and barx1 within sox10:GFP+ domains along the posterior pharyngeal arches (white arrowheads) and fin bud mesenchyme (yellow arrowheads) at both time points (Figure 3F–K,M–R).
evidence: This is a finding from the HCR validation.

claim: Cells with NCC identity were detected in Cluster 5 at 48–50 hpf, defined by expression of the core NCC markers sox10, foxd3, crestin, and tfap2a.
source: At 48–50 hpf, cells with NCC identity were notably detected in Cluster 5, defined by expression of the core NCC markers sox10, foxd3, crestin, and tfap2a (Figure 1F; Figure 4, Figure 1—source data 2; Dutton et al., 2001; Luo et al., 2001; Knight et al., 2003; Stewart et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis supported by citations.

claim: Cluster 5 contained various other genes previously shown to be expressed in zebrafish NCCs, including vim, snai1b, sox9b, zeb2a, mych, and mmp17b.
source: Moreover, Cluster five was found to contain various other genes previously shown to be expressed in zebrafish NCCs; including, vim, snai1b, sox9b, zeb2a, mych, and mmp17b (Figure 4D; Cerdà et al., 1998; Heffer et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2008; Leigh et al., 2013; Van Otterloo et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2011; Rocha et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis supported by citations.

claim: Enteric markers in zebrafish include sox10, phox2bb, ret, gfra1a, meis3, and zeb2a.
source: Enteric markers in zebrafish include sox10, phox2bb, ret, gfra1a, meis3, and zeb2a (Dutton et al., 2001; Shepherd et al., 2004; Elworthy et al., 2005; Delalande et al., 2008; Heanue and Pachnis, 2008; Uribe and Bronner, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Within Cluster 5, expression of the enteric markers phox2bb, ret, gfra1a, meis3, sox10, and zeb2a was observed.
source: Therefore, we expected to capture a population of ENCCs within our 48–50 hpf dataset. Indeed, within Cluster 5 we observed expression of the enteric markers phox2bb, ret, gfra1a, meis3, sox10, and zeb2a (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Gene orthologs known to be expressed in ENCC in amniotes, such as ngfrb (orthologue to p75) and hoxb5b (orthologous to Hoxb5), were detected within Cluster 5.
source: Furthermore, gene orthologs known to be expressed in ENCC in amniotes were detected within Cluster 5, such as ngfrb (orthologue to p75; Anderson et al., 2006; Wilson et al., 2004) and hoxb5b (orthologous to Hoxb5; Kam and Lui, 2015; Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis supported by citations.

claim: HCR analysis of 48 hpf embryos validated the co-expression profiles of several ENCC markers along the foregut.
source: HCR analysis of 48 hpf embryos validated the co-expression profiles of several ENCC markers along the foregut (Figure 4E–F; foregut in gray box). We observed that a chain of crestin+ cells localized in the foregut contained a subpopulation of cells expressing ngfrb, phox2bb, and gfra1a (Figure 4E; white arrowheads), or expressing foxd3, ngfrb, and gfra1a (Figure 4F; white arrowheads).
evidence: This is a finding from the HCR validation.

claim: Differentiating enteric neurons were identified within the 68–70 hpf dataset based on the combinatorial expression of elavl3, phox2bb, ret, and gfra1a.
source: We identified differentiating enteric neurons within the 68–70 hpf dataset based on the combinatorial expression of elavl3, phox2bb, ret, and gfra1a (Figure 4G), which mapped to the neural/neuronal major cell type regions of the dataset (Figure 1E), comprising Clusters 5 and 12 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Transcripts that encode for the neurochemical marker nos1, and the neuropeptides vip and vipb, were found in a subpopulation of enteric neurons localized to a distal group of the neuronal cluster.
source: Transcripts that encode for the neurochemical marker nos1, and the neuropeptides vip and vipb, a paralogue to vip (Gaudet et al., 2011), were found in a subpopulation of enteric neurons localized to a distal group of the neuronal cluster, likely indicative of a differentiating enteric neuron subtype (Figure 4G; red arrows).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis supported by a citation.

claim: The pan-neuronal markers tuba2, elavl3, stx1b, and gng2/3 were present in both Clusters 5 and 12.
source: The pan-neuronal markers tuba2, elavl3, stx1b, and gng2/3 (Asakawa and Kawakami, 2010; Kelly et al., 2008; Park et al., 2000; Zheng et al., 2018), as well as the autonomic neuron markers, phox2a and phox2bb (Hans et al., 2013), were present in both Clusters 5 and 12 (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis supported by citations.

claim: The enteric neuron markers, gfra1a, ret, hoxb5b, ngfrb, fgf13b, nos1, vipb, and vip were mostly confined to Cluster 12.
source: However, the enteric neuron markers, gfra1a, ret, hoxb5b, ngfrb, fgf13b, nos1, vipb, and vip were mostly confined to Cluster 12, suggesting that this cluster contained differentiating enteric neurons (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Whole mount HCR analysis validated the spatiotemporal co-expression of phox2bb, nos1, vipb, and elavl3 transcripts throughout the foregut of the zebrafish embryo by 69 hpf.
source: Indeed, whole mount HCR analysis validated the spatiotemporal co-expression of phox2bb, nos1, vipb, and elavl3 transcripts throughout the foregut of the zebrafish embryo by 69 hpf (Figure 4I; yellow arrowheads).
evidence: This is a finding from the HCR validation.

claim: elavl3+/phox2bb+ early differentiating enteric neurons are first seen in the foregut and display an inhibitory neurochemical gene signature.
source: These results suggest that elavl3+/phox2bb+ early differentiating enteric neurons are first seen in the foregut and display an inhibitory neurochemical gene signature, consistent with prior observations in zebrafish and mammalian ENS (Olden et al., 2008; Hao and Young, 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by citations.

claim: Clusters 5 and 12 were subset from the main 68-70 hpf dataset, re-clustered and visualized using a tSNE plot, producing 5 Sub-clusters.
source: In an effort to examine the enteric neuron populations with finer resolution, Clusters 5 and 12 were subset from the main dataset in Seurat, re-clustered and visualized using a tSNE plot, producing 5 Sub-clusters (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the data analysis procedure.

claim: Sub-cluster 3 was identified as a differentiated enteric neuron cluster.
source: The previously mentioned enteric neuron markers, with the addition of etv1, a recently identified marker of an enteric sensory neuron type, intrinsic primary afferent neurons (IPANs) in mouse (Morarach et al., 2021), were queried and visualized using dot and feature plot allowing the identification of Sub-cluster 3 as a differentiated enteric neuron cluster (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the sub-cluster analysis supported by a citation.

claim: nos1, vip, and vipb were enriched in Sub-cluster 3.
source: nos1, vip, and vipb were enriched in Sub-cluster 3 (Figure 5B,C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the sub-cluster analysis.

claim: Sub-cluster 1 formed a central point from which Sub-cluster 3 could be seen emanating as a distal population.
source: Sub-cluster 1 formed a central point from which Sub-cluster 3 could be seen emanating as a distal population (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from the tSNE visualization.

claim: Sub-clusters 1 and 3 likely depict enteric neurons captured at different stages along their progressive differentiation.
source: Sub-clusters 1 and 3 likely depict enteric neurons captured at different stages along their progressive differentiation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sub-cluster analysis.

claim: Within a small pocket of cells in Sub-cluster 3, expression of calb2a and pbx3b was detected.
source: Within a small pocket of cells in Sub-cluster 3, we detected the expression of calb2a and pbx3b (Figure 5D,E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1), orthologous genes to Calb2 and Pbx3 that have previously been shown to denote adult myenteric IPANs in mammals (Furness et al., 2004; Memic et al., 2018), as well as the two acetylcholine associated genes, acetylcholine esterase (ache, Bertrand et al., 2001; Huang et al., 2019) and vesicular acetylcholine transferase (slc18a3a, Hong et al., 2013; Zoli and Berlin, 2000; Figure 5E; red arrowheads).
evidence: This is a finding from the sub-cluster analysis supported by citations.

claim: A scRNA-seq study performed in E15.5 mouse demonstrated the co-expression of Calb2, Pbx3, and Slc18a during ENS development.
source: Recently, a scRNA-seq study performed in E15.5 mouse demonstrated the co-expression of Calb2, Pbx3, and Slc18a during ENS development (Morarach et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: HCR analysis revealed co-expression of pbx3b, calb2a, vipb, and nos1 in discrete differentiating enteric neurons within the foregut region of the zebrafish gut at 68 hpf.
source: When examining IPAN gene markers in zebrafish larvae, HCR analysis revealed co-expression of pbx3b, calb2a, vipb, and nos1 (Figure 5G; white arrowheads), or co-expression of slc18a3a, calb2a, vipb, and nos1 (Figure 5G; yellow arrowheads), in discrete differentiating enteric neurons within the foregut region of the zebrafish gut at 68 hpf.
evidence: This is a finding from the HCR validation.

claim: Zebrafish differentiating enteric neurons express IPAN gene signatures during their development.
source: These data indicate that zebrafish differentiating enteric neurons express IPAN gene signatures during their development.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HCR validation data.

claim: The sox10:GFP+68–70 hpf dataset captured an emerging IPAN population during its transition, where both excitatory and inhibitory neurochemical markers were co-expressed.
source: Collectively, our observations suggest that the sox10:GFP+68–70 hpf dataset captured an emerging IPAN population during its transition, where both excitatory and inhibitory neurochemical markers were co-expressed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data analysis.

claim: The transcriptional emergence of specific enteric neuron subtypes may be conserved between vertebrate species.
source: Therefore, our single-cell analysis in zebrafish suggests that the transcriptional emergence of specific enteric neuron subtypes may be conserved between vertebrate species.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings suggesting evolutionary conservation.

claim: Three opioid signaling pathways were among the top 10 highest fold enriched pathways in Sub-cluster 3.
source: In order to identify novel signaling pathways within the developing enteric neuron population, the significantly enriched gene list from Sub-cluster 3 was processed using gene ontology (GO) pathway enrichment analysis. We found that three opioid signaling pathways were among the top 10 highest fold enriched pathways (Figure 5—source data 2; Mi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the GO pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: These opioid signaling pathways contained the G-protein-coupled receptors, oprl1 and oprd1b.
source: These pathways contained the G-protein-coupled receptors, oprl1 and oprd1b, respectively representing nociception/orphan FQ (N/OFQ) peptide (NOP)-receptor and delta-opioid receptor (DOR) subtype members within the opioid receptor superfamily (Figure 5H; Donica et al., 2013; Sobczak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway analysis supported by citations.

claim: Expression of the opioid receptors was tightly confined within the pocket of enteric neuron progenitors identified as undergoing sensory lineage-specification.
source: Specifically, feature plots showed that expression of the opioid receptors was tightly confined within the pocket of enteric neuron progenitors we identified as undergoing sensory lineage-specification, suggesting the expression of opioid receptor genes within both excitatory and inhibitory neurons at the early stages of enteric neuron differentiation within the zebrafish ENS (Figure 5E and H).
evidence: This is a finding from the feature plot analysis.

claim: HCR analysis confirmed the combinatorial expression of oprl1, vipb, and phox2bb within migrating enteric neuron progenitors at 68 hpf along the foregut.
source: Confirming this suggestion using HCR analysis, we observed the combinatorial expression of oprl1, vipb, and phox2bb within migrating enteric neuron progenitors at 68 hpf along the foregut (Figure 5I–N).
evidence: This is a finding from the HCR validation.

claim: The presence of opioid receptors within immature enteric neurons undergoing lineage-specification highlights an area that requires further investigation.
source: The presence of opioid receptors within immature enteric neurons undergoing lineage-specification helps us to better understand the complexity of early ENS signaling and highlights an area that requires further investigation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings and a suggestion for future research.

claim: UMAP analysis allowed better visualization of the separation between the Sub-clusters.
source: In order to better visualize specific differences between the Sub-clusters, we viewed them using UMAP (Becht et al., 2019; Mcinnes et al., 2018; Figure 5—figure supplement 2). While the identity of the previous tSNE Sub-clusters were maintained, UMAP analysis allowed us to better visualize the separation between the Sub-clusters, which we were able to broadly classify as autonomic neurons based on their shared expression of ascl1a, hand2, phox2a, and phox2bb (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B,D).
evidence: This describes the UMAP analysis procedure and results.

claim: A population of sympathetic neurons was distinguished within Sub-cluster 2 based on their combinatorial expression of th, dbh, lmo1, and insm1a.
source: Within the population of autonomic neurons, we were able to distinguish a population of sympathetic neurons within Sub-cluster 2 based on their combinatorial expression of th, dbh, lmo1, and insm1a (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,E), which could be clearly distinguished from the enteric neuron Sub-cluster 3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the UMAP analysis.

claim: Sub-cluster 0 appears as a common sympatho-enteric neuron pool that lacks the expression of sympathetic and enteric specific neurochemical markers.
source: Taking together the architecture of the UMAP clusters and their respective gene expression signatures, Sub-cluster 0 appears as a common sympatho-enteric neuron pool that lacks the expression of sympathetic and enteric specific neurochemical markers (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the UMAP analysis.

claim: Sub-clusters 1 and 4 emanate as two distinct populations from Sub-cluster 0 and respectively exhibit lower expression levels of sympathetic and enteric markers comparative to the sympathetic and enteric neuron Sub-clusters 2 and 3.
source: Sub-clusters 1 and 4 emanate as two distinct populations from Sub-cluster 0 and respectively exhibit lower expression levels of sympathetic and enteric markers comparative to the sympathetic and enteric neuron Sub-clusters 2 and 3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B,E,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the UMAP analysis.

claim: Sub-cluster 0 cells may represent a pool of immature sympatho-enteric neurons.
source: Overall, these results suggest that Sub-cluster 0 cells may represent a pool of immature sympatho-enteric neurons, and that Sub-clusters 1 and 4 both represent further differentiated, yet still immature, pools of enteric and sympathetic neurons captured during the process of lineage specification into their respective terminal enteric and sympathetic neuron populations represented in Sub-clusters 3 and 2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the UMAP analysis.

claim: The 48–50 hpf and 68–70 hpf datasets were merged using Seurat's dataset and Integration and Label Transfer utility.
source: To describe the dynamic transcriptional relationship between sox10:GFP+ cells across both time points, we merged the 48–50 hpf and 68–70 hpf datasets using Seurat's dataset and Integration and Label Transfer utility (Stuart et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the data integration procedure.

claim: The merged datasets were visualized via UMAP, where 27 clusters were detected.
source: The merged datasets were visualized via UMAP, where we detected 27 clusters (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the visualization and clustering results.

claim: Every cluster identified in the 48–50 hpf dataset mapped proximally to clusters at 68–70 hpf.
source: We observed that every cluster identified in the 48–50 hpf dataset mapped proximally to clusters at 68–70 hpf (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the merged atlas analysis.

claim: 48h-Cluster 2 and 68h-Cluster 8 both showed a high degree of similarity, as well as consistent barx1, dlx2a, and twist1a expression.
source: Illustrating this point, 48h-Cluster 2 and 68h-Cluster 8 both showed a high degree of similarity, as well as consistent barx1, dlx2a, and twist1a expression (Figure 6B), consistent with our prior analysis (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the merged atlas analysis.

claim: The early specified melanophore population at 48h-Cluster 8 branched into later stage melanophore populations (68h-Clusters 4 and 18).
source: Specifically, we observed the early specified melanophore population at 48h-Cluster 8 branched into later stage melanophore populations (68h-Clusters 4 and 18).
evidence: This is a finding from the merged atlas analysis.

claim: The common bi-potent pigment progenitor population (68h-Cluster 13) bridged both melanophore clusters and the iridophore 68h-Cluster 16.
source: Further, we observed that the common bi-potent pigment progenitor population (68h-Cluster 13) bridged both melanophore clusters and the iridophore 68h-Cluster 16.
evidence: This is a finding from the merged atlas analysis.

claim: Cells within the neural/neuronal clusters assembled such that progenitor cells bridged into differentiating neurons spatially from the top to the bottom of the neural/neuronal region of the atlas.
source: Cells within the neural/neuronal clusters assembled such that progenitor cells bridged into differentiating neurons spatially from the top to the bottom of the neural/neuronal region of the atlas (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the merged atlas analysis.

claim: The 68–70 hpf neural progenitor populations (Clusters 3 and 10) shared common gene expression with the 48–50 hpf NCC population (48h-Cluster 5), reflected largely by their co-expression of sox10, notch1a, dla, and foxd3.
source: Of interest, the 68–70 hpf neural progenitor populations (Clusters 3 and 10) shared common gene expression with the 48–50 hpf NCC population (48h-Cluster 5), reflected largely by their co-expression of sox10, notch1a, dla, and foxd3 (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the merged atlas analysis.

claim: The spatiotemporal expression domains of notch1a and dla were confirmed along the hindbrain, spinal cord, and in NCC populations along the post-otic vagal domain at 48 hpf.
source: We confirmed the spatiotemporal expression domains of notch1a and dla along the hindbrain, spinal cord, and in NCC populations along the post-otic vagal domain at 48 hpf (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F; arrowheads), in particular with dla in the ENCCs along the foregut (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F; arrow), a pattern similar to the ENCC makers sox10 and phox2bb (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the in situ hybridization validation.

claim: A bifurcation in cell states was observed delineated from the neural progenitor cells, with one moving toward a Schwann/glial cell fate, while the other branched toward neuronal.
source: Delineated from the neural progenitor cells, we observed a bifurcation in cell states; with one moving toward a Schwann/glial cell fate, while the other branched toward neuronal.
evidence: This is a finding from the merged atlas analysis.

claim: The glial arm followed a temporal progression of earlier cell fates at 48–50 hpf (48h-Cluster 15) toward the more mature fates at 68–70 hpf (68h-Cluster 14), both denoted by expression of olig2 and pou3f1, respectively.
source: The glial arm followed a temporal progression of earlier cell fates at 48–50 hpf (48h-Cluster 15) toward the more mature fates at 68–70 hpf (68h-Cluster 14), both denoted by expression of olig2 and pou3f1, respectively (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the merged atlas analysis.

claim: Enteric progenitors culminated into a pool of enteric neurons, with the specific neural signature: vipb, nos1, gfra1a, fgf13b, and etv1.
source: For example, enteric progenitors culminated into a pool of enteric neurons, with the specific neural signature: vipb, nos1, gfra1a, fgf13b, and etv1 (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the merged atlas analysis.

claim: The xanthophore differentiation marker xdh demonstrated expected restriction in expression to 68–70 hpf.
source: For example, while the xanthophore differentiation marker xdh demonstrated expected restriction in expression to 68–70 hpf, we identified genes with no known roles in pigment cell development differentially expressed between the two stages, such as rgs16 and SMIM18 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Genes with no known roles in pigment cell development, such as rgs16 and SMIM18, were identified as differentially expressed between the two stages.
source: For example, while the xanthophore differentiation marker xdh demonstrated expected restriction in expression to 68–70 hpf, we identified genes with no known roles in pigment cell development differentially expressed between the two stages, such as rgs16 and SMIM18 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Within the mesenchyme lineages, both barx1 and snai1b followed expected temporal expression trends.
source: Moreover, within the mesenchyme lineages, both barx1 and snai1b followed expected temporal expression trends, while abracl and id1 both demonstrated novel differential gene expression profiles within the mesenchyme (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: abracl and id1 both demonstrated novel differential gene expression profiles within the mesenchyme.
source: Moreover, within the mesenchyme lineages, both barx1 and snai1b followed expected temporal expression trends, while abracl and id1 both demonstrated novel differential gene expression profiles within the mesenchyme (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: The neural/neuronal lineage showed expected differential gene expression of genes such as etv1 and vipb at 68–70 hpf.
source: Lastly, the neural/neuronal lineage showed expected differential gene expression of genes such as etv1 and vipb at 68–70 hpf, while revealing novel expression of nova2 and zgc:162730, which have previously uncharacterized roles in sox10-derived cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: nova2 and zgc:162730 have previously uncharacterized roles in sox10-derived cells.
source: Lastly, the neural/neuronal lineage showed expected differential gene expression of genes such as etv1 and vipb at 68–70 hpf, while revealing novel expression of nova2 and zgc:162730, which have previously uncharacterized roles in sox10-derived cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: 45 of the 49 zebrafish hox genes were detected across the atlas.
source: We detected broad expression of 45 of the 49 zebrafish hox genes across the atlas, with 85% of the cells in the atlas expressing at least one hox gene (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,J).
evidence: This is a finding from the hox gene analysis.

claim: 85% of the cells in the atlas expressed at least one hox gene.
source: We detected broad expression of 45 of the 49 zebrafish hox genes across the atlas, with 85% of the cells in the atlas expressing at least one hox gene (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,J).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the hox gene analysis.

claim: Specific hox gene expression patterns demarcated distinct tissues, with specific robustness in the neural fated cells.
source: A dot plot revealed that specific hox gene expression patterns demarcated distinct tissues, with specific robustness in the neural fated cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding from the hox gene analysis.

claim: A core hox profile was common to the neural lineages, which included hoxb1b, hoxc1a, hoxb2a, hoxb3a, hoxc3a, hoxd3a, hoxa4a, hoxd4a, hoxb5a, hoxb5b, hoxc5a, hoxb6a, hoxb6b, and hoxb8a.
source: Common to the neural lineages, we observed a core hox profile which included hoxb1b, hoxc1a, hoxb2a, hoxb3a, hoxc3a, hoxd3a, hoxa4a, hoxd4a, hoxb5a, hoxb5b, hoxc5a, hoxb6a, hoxb6b, and hoxb8a (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding from the hox gene analysis.

claim: hoxa4a was widely expressed in several lineages.
source: One of the top expressed constituents of the core signature, hoxa4a, was also widely expressed in several other lineages (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the hox gene analysis.

claim: Clustering of all the atlas lineages relying only on hox gene expression highlighted the robustness of the core hox signature to distinguish the neural lineage fates.
source: Clustering of all the atlas lineages relying only on hox gene expression highlighted the robustness of the core hox signature to distinguish the neural lineage fates, grouping the differentiating (autonomic neuronal progenitors, enteric neurons, enteric progenitors and CNS neurons) and progenitor lineages (neural progenitors and glial progenitors) into neighboring clades (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from the hox-based clustering analysis.

claim: There was a detectable shift in hox expression among the autonomic neural progenitors to the enteric neuronal lineage, demarcated by the increase in hoxb2a, hoxd4a, hoxa5a, hoxb5a, and hoxb5b, accompanied by diminished expression of hoxc3a, hoxc5a, hoxb6a and hoxb8a.
source: Most notably, considering the lineages in increasing specificity of cell fate, there was a detectable shift in hox expression among the autonomic neural progenitors to the enteric neuronal lineage, demarcated by the increase in hoxb2a, hoxd4a, hoxa5a, hoxb5a, and hoxb5b, accompanied by diminished expression of hoxc3a, hoxc5a, hoxb6a and hoxb8a, which formed a distinctive enteric hox signature (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,K–N).
evidence: This is a finding from the hox gene analysis.

claim: The enteric neural hox signature was not only specific to this cell population, but also was abundantly co-expressed.
source: Examining the autonomic neuronal progenitors (Figure 7C) and the enteric neuron populations (Figure 7D), both lineages demonstrated pervasive fractions of co-positive cells for combinations of the core hox signature.
evidence: This is a finding from the pairwise hox gene analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The enteric signature was highly enriched in the unique expression of hoxa5a, with co-expression for hoxb5a (36%) and hoxb5b (36%), as well as strong co-expression of hoxd4a or hoxb5a with hoxb5b.
source: The enteric signature was highly enriched in the unique expression of hoxa5a, with co-expression for hoxb5a (36%) and hoxb5b (36%), as well as strong co-expression of hoxd4a or hoxb5a with hoxb5b (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the pairwise hox gene analysis.

claim: At 70–72 hpf, enteric neurons along the level of the midgut, marked by phox2bb expression, were hoxb5a+/hoxb5b+ and hoxd4a+/hoxa5a+.
source: At 70–72 hpf, as predicted by our analysis, enteric neurons along the level of the midgut, marked by phox2bb expression (Figure 7F,J), were hoxb5a+/hoxb5b+ (Figure 7G–I) and hoxd4a+/hoxa5a+ (Figure 7K–M).
evidence: This is a finding from the HCR validation.

claim: Enteric neurons co-express enteric hox code genes during their early development.
source: These data confirm that enteric neurons co-express enteric hox code genes during their early development.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HCR validation data.

claim: Both the chondrogenic and general mesenchyme clusters demonstrated hoxa2b expression, as well as weak expression for hoxb2a, hoxb3a, and hoxd4a.
source: With respect to the remaining cluster identities (Figure 7A), many of the populations showed varied hox expression profiles. Both the chondrogenic and general mesenchyme clusters demonstrated hoxa2b expression, as well as weak expression for hoxb2a, hoxb3a, and hoxd4a.
evidence: This is a finding from the hox gene analysis.

claim: The detection of hoxa2b, hoxb2a, hoxb3a, and hoxd4a expression profiles was consistent with prior reports that they are expressed within NCC targets toward the posterior pharyngeal arches, as well as migrating NCC.
source: Our detection of these hox expression profiles was consistent with prior reports that they are expressed within NCC targets toward the posterior pharyngeal arches, as well as migrating NCC (Minoux and Rijli, 2010; Parker et al., 2018; Parker et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The distinct identity of the fin bud mesenchyme was detected through the expression of hoxa9b, hoxa10b, hoxa11b, hoxa13b, hoxd9a, and hoxd12a.
source: We detected the distinct identity of the fin bud mesenchyme (Ahn and Ho, 2008; Nakamura et al., 2016) through the expression of hoxa9b, hoxa10b, hoxa11b, hoxa13b, hoxd9a, and hoxd12a (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1P–Q).
evidence: This is a finding from the hox gene analysis supported by citations.

claim: The pigment populations, including the pigment progenitors, melanophores, iridophores, and xanthophores, contained generally low levels of hox gene expression.
source: The pigment populations, including the pigment progenitors, melanophores, iridophores, and xanthophores, contained generally low levels of hox gene expression.
evidence: This is a finding from the hox gene analysis.

claim: Low levels of hoxa4a, hoxb7a, hoxb8a, hoxc3a, and hoxd4a were detected among the iridophore population.
source: For example, low levels of hoxa4a, hoxb7a, hoxb8a, hoxc3a, and hoxd4a were detected among the iridophore population, while only hoxb7a was detected within a high fraction of xanthophores (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the hox gene analysis.

claim: Only hoxb7a was detected within a high fraction of xanthophores.
source: For example, low levels of hoxa4a, hoxb7a, hoxb8a, hoxc3a, and hoxd4a were detected among the iridophore population, while only hoxb7a was detected within a high fraction of xanthophores (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the hox gene analysis.

claim: The melanophore population displayed uniformly very low levels of detectable hox expression.
source: Interestingly, these expression profiles are not shared by the melanophore population, which displayed uniformly very low levels of detectable hox expression.
evidence: This is a finding from the hox gene analysis.

claim: The muscle, otic, and unidentified cells showed almost no hox expression profile.
source: Lastly, the muscle, otic, and unidentified cells showed almost no hox expression profile, which serves a foil for the specificity of the signatures outlined.
evidence: This is a finding from the hox gene analysis.

claim: The 'pigmented muscle' cluster weakly mirrored the general neural hox signature, likely a shared signature more reflective of the axial position of the muscle cells rather than a shared genetic profile.
source: We noted that the 'pigmented muscle' cluster weakly mirrored the general neural hox signature, likely a shared signature more reflective of the axial position of the muscle cells rather than a shared genetic profile, as corroborated by their distinct separation of the clusters on the atlas UMAP (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hox gene analysis.

claim: Distinct cell types express unique hox combinations during their delineation.
source: Overall, these above described hox signatures detected within our scRNA-seq atlas indicates that distinct cell types express unique hox combinations during their delineation.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the hox gene analysis.

claim: This study is the first single-cell transcriptomic analysis covering early ENS development in zebrafish.
source: Our study is the first single-cell transcriptomic analysis covering early ENS development in zebrafish, in addition to analysis of posterior sox10+ mesenchyme and pigment cells present during the late embryonic to larval phase.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The developmental window examined, the embryonic to larval transition, is regarded as an ephemeral phase.
source: The developmental window we examined, the embryonic to larval transition, is regarded as an ephemeral phase (Singleman and Holtzman, 2014) and as such is expected to contain the dynamic cell differentiation states that we observed within our atlas.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Distinct hox transcriptional codes demarcate differentiating neural and neuronal populations.
source: We discovered that distinct hox transcriptional codes demarcate differentiating neural and neuronal populations, highlighting their potential roles during cell subtype specification.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the study.

claim: The study uncovered evolutionarily conserved and novel transcriptional signatures of differentiating enteric neuron cell types.
source: We uncovered evolutionarily conserved and novel transcriptional signatures of differentiating enteric neuron cell types, thereby expanding our knowledge of ENS development.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the study.

claim: A similar enteric population consisting of Sox10, Ret, Phox2b, and Elavl4 was identified by scRNA-seq in the mouse.
source: Collectively, our single-cell datasets captured the transition from enteric neural progenitor to differentiating enteric neuron subtype (Figures 4, 5 and 6). A similar enteric population consisting of Sox10, Ret, Phox2b, and Elavl4 was identified by scRNA-seq in the mouse (Lasrado et al., 2017), indicating zebrafish express conserved enteric programs.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A recent scRNA-seq study performed using E15.5 mice suggests that Nos1+/Vip+ cells represent a post-mitotic immature neuron population capable of branching into excitatory and inhibitory neurons via subsequent differentiation mediated by lineage-restricted gene expression.
source: As well, a recent scRNA-seq study performed using E15.5 mice, a time point further along in ENS development when compared to our zebrafish study described here, suggests that Nos1+/Vip+ cells represent a post-mitotic immature neuron population capable of branching into excitatory and inhibitory neurons via subsequent differentiation mediated by lineage-restricted gene expression (Morarach et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The model of IPAN formation proposed by Morarach et al., 2021 posits that Nos1+/Vip+/Gal+ enteric neurons are capable of assuming an IPAN signature, characterized by the loss of Vip and Nos1, and the gain of Calb, Slc18a2/3, and Ntng1; a process regulated by transcription factors, Pbx3 and Etv1.
source: Their model posits that Nos1+/Vip+/Gal+ enteric neurons are capable of assuming an IPAN signature, characterized by the loss of Vip and Nos1, and the gain of Calb, Slc18a2/3, and Ntng1; a process regulated by transcription factors, Pbx3 and Etv1.
evidence: This describes a model from prior research.

claim: The observations in zebrafish corroborate the proposed mammalian gene expression model of IPAN formation.
source: Our observations in zebrafish (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 6) corroborates the proposed mammalian gene expression model and suggests that we captured a transitional time point where subsequent differentiation is just being initiated (Figure 5F) and suggests an evolutionarily conserved mechanism of ENS formation across vertebrate species.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings suggesting evolutionary conservation.

claim: The expression of opioid receptors has previously been shown in inhibitory interneurons found within the adult ENS where they are known to play functional roles during gut homeostasis.
source: The expression of opioid receptors has previously been shown in inhibitory interneurons found within the adult ENS where they are known to play functional roles during gut homeostasis (DiCello et al., 2020; Lay et al., 2016; Wood and Galligan, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A recent study performed in zebrafish found that oprl1 was expressed within 7 dpf enteric neurons following bulk RNA sequencing.
source: Indeed, a recent study performed in zebrafish found that oprl1 was expressed within 7 dpf enteric neurons following bulk RNA sequencing (Roy-Carson et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The 68–70 hpf dataset represents the earliest stage in which oprl1 and oprd1b have been shown to be expressed within the early developing ENS.
source: As such, our 68–70 hpf dataset, in which we detected the expression of oprl1 and oprd1b, represents the earliest stage in which they have been shown to be expressed within the early developing ENS.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior research.

claim: The presence of opioid receptor transcripts within the ENS at 68–70 hpf highlights an important area of research focusing on the interplay between opioid use and fetal ENS development.
source: The presence of opioid receptor transcripts within the ENS at 68–70 hpf, a time when immature enteric neurons are continuing to migrate and pattern within the developing embryo, highlights an important area of research focusing on the interplay between opioid use and fetal ENS development, a reality that has been on the rise in recent decades as opioid abuse continues to increase.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings and a suggestion for future research.

claim: A comprehensive, combinatorial code of hox expression defines specific cell lineages within the context of the sox10 atlas.
source: Finally, we have elucidated a comprehensive, combinatorial code of hox expression which defines specific cell lineages within the context of the sox10 atlas.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the study.

claim: The fin bud mesenchyme, pigment populations, and neural fates presented the most specific hox codes.
source: The fin bud mesenchyme, pigment populations, and neural fates presented the most specific hox codes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the hox gene analysis.

claim: A previously undescribed hox signature demarcating the developing enteric neuron population in zebrafish was identified: high relative expression of hoxb2a, hoxa5a, hoxd4a, hoxb5a, and hoxb5b, while also exhibiting low expression of hoxc3a, hoxc5a, hoxb6a, and hoxb8a.
source: Among the neural lineages, we identified a previously undescribed hox signature demarcating the developing enteric neuron population in zebrafish: high relative expression of hoxb2a, hoxa5a, hoxd4a, hoxb5a, and hoxb5b, while also exhibiting low expression of hoxc3a, hoxc5a, hoxb6a, and hoxb8a (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the hox gene analysis.

claim: Previous bulk microarray studies of differentiating enteric neurons from humans and mice have been shown to express orthologs to the enteric hox signature.
source: While previous bulk microarray studies of differentiating enteric neurons from humans and mice have been shown to express orthologs to the former signature (Heanue and Pachnis, 2008; Memic et al., 2018), our analysis extends knowledge to comprehensively show for the first time specific combinatorial hox expression at a single-cell resolution, thereby providing a heretofore unknown readout of hox heterogeneity among nascent enteric cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The conservation of an enteric hox signature between zebrafish and other systems points toward a larger conservation of function.
source: The conservation of an enteric hox signature between zebrafish and other systems points toward a larger conservation of function, which may facilitate translation of future findings between models.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings suggesting evolutionary conservation.

claim: Overlapping expression domains of hox genes may facilitate enteric neural subtype differentiation, similar to their function in hindbrain and spinal neurons.
source: Considered collectively, these data lend support to a model in which overlapping expression domains of hox genes may facilitate enteric neural subtype differentiation, similar to their function in hindbrain and spinal neurons (Philippidou and Dasen, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings supported by a citation.

claim: The study greatly increases foundational understanding of NCC-derived cell fates, as well as other sox10+ posterior cell types in zebrafish.
source: In summary, our study greatly increases foundational understanding of NCC-derived cell fates, as well as other sox10+posterior cell types in zebrafish, thereby complementing ongoing studies in mammalian models and expanding fundamental knowledge of how cells diversify in developing organisms.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the study's contribution.

claim: The spatiotemporal information contained within the zebrafish atlas will serve as a resource for the developmental biology, stem cell, evolutionary biology and organogenesis communities.
source: The spatiotemporal information contained within our zebrafish atlas will serve as a resource for the developmental biology, stem cell, evolutionary biology and organogenesis communities.
evidence: This is a statement about the intended use of the atlas.
